accroche: Losing 90% of your brain would be painless, the legend says; the organ's energy bill says the opposite.
contenu_vulgarise:
A human brain weighs about 1.4 kilograms. If the received idea were true, that we use only a tenth of it, we could lose the other nine tenths without losing anything essential. No neurosurgeon would sign that sentence.

## An Energy Bill That Does Not Add Up

The brain accounts for about 2% of body mass. Yet it consumes about 20% of the oxygen used by the body at rest, according to reference data in neurochemistry. An organ this costly to run would not sit 90% idle: evolution would long since have trimmed the excess.

Modern imaging confirms this reasoning. Electroencephalogram, positron emission tomography, functional MRI: none of these techniques shows vast silent areas waiting for future use. The resting brain is already regulating breathing, temperature, attention, memory; there is no “reserve zone.”

Clinical practice says the same thing in another way. A lesion, even a small one, in a precise area of the brain produces measurable and often lasting effects: loss of speech, of a portion of the visual field, of the ability to recognize a face. If 90% of the brain served no purpose, these tiny lesions would have no consequence. They never lack one.

## Where Does the Legend Come From, Then?

The myth often latches onto the name of the psychologist William James. In 1907, in *The Energies of Men*, James writes that most people exploit only a small part of their possible mental and physical resources, a remark about untapped potential, not a numerical claim about gray matter. No percentage, no neuron.

The distortion probably comes from elsewhere. In 1936, the author Lowell Thomas writes the preface to *How to Win Friends and Influence People*, by Dale Carnegie, and there attributes to James the idea that human beings develop only 10% of their latent mental abilities. The figure was born there, or thereabouts, then it traveled, detaching from its context, until it became a neuroscientific statistic that never existed.

The myth survives so well because it flatters: it promises an immense reserve of hidden potential, available to anyone who could unlock it. The reality is less marketable, and more interesting, an organ that wastes nothing, where every damaged area is paid for in cash.

repere.texte: The brain accounts for only about 2% of body mass, but it consumes about 20% of the oxygen used by the whole body at rest.
repere.source: Clarke, D.D. & Sokoloff, L., “Regulation of Cerebral Metabolic Rate,” in Basic Neurochemistry, 6th ed., 1999 (NCBI Bookshelf)

carte.punch: The 10% brain myth does not survive its own energy bill.
carte.idee: The brain weighs only 2% of the body but consumes about 20% of its energy at rest. No imaging shows an inactive area, and the slightest lesion has measurable effects. The “10%” figure comes from a 1936 preface wrongly attributed to William James.

quiz.question: Why is the energy argument enough to dismiss the idea that 90% of the brain is unused?
choix: Because the brain consumes almost no energy, so its activity does not show
Because inactive neurons end up disappearing before adulthood
Because an organ this costly to run would not sit 90% idle without evolution having reduced it
Because the brain repairs itself when an area is not used
quiz.explication: The brain is a very energy-costly organ: being 90% inactive would be incompatible with natural selection, and brain lesions, even small ones, always have measurable effects, proof that no area is superfluous.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the electroencephalogram, positron emission tomography, and functional MRI show about brain activity?
choix: Vast areas of the brain stay permanently silent
Only the left half of the brain shows measurable activity
None of these techniques shows an inactive area waiting for future use
Brain activity drops sharply after age forty
quiz_supplementaire.explication: None of these imaging techniques reveals vast silent areas waiting for future use: the resting brain is already regulating breathing, temperature, attention, and memory.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does a brain lesion, even a small one, cause, according to the entry?
choix: Measurable and often lasting effects, such as loss of speech
No notable effect if it affects less than 10% of the brain
A temporary improvement in certain cognitive abilities
Effects only if it affects more than 50% of the brain
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A lesion, even a tiny one, produces measurable and often lasting effects, loss of speech, of a portion of the visual field, or of the ability to recognize a face, proof that no area is superfluous.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did William James actually write in 1907, in The Energies of Men?
choix: That the human brain uses only 10% of its capacities
That most people exploit only a small part of their possible mental and physical resources, with no precise figure
That 90% of the brain stays inactive throughout life
That only certain professions fully develop their brains
quiz_supplementaire.explication: James speaks of untapped potential in most people, putting forward no percentage and saying nothing of gray matter: the 10% figure appears only in 1936, in a preface that wrongly attributes it to him.
